case_info.scenario: A male infant aged 2 weeks presented to an otolaryngology clinic for evaluation of a tongue lesion. The patient was born at 39 weeks of gestation via caesarean delivery that was complicated by preeclampsia. Prenatal ultrasonography and subsequent magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated concern for a tongue cyst. At birth, a small midline tongue defect was noted, for which the patient was referred to an ear, nose, and throat clinic. At the time of the initial evaluation, he was feeding well and gaining weight appropriately. He was found to have a shallow, midline tongue depression with no discrete masses or lesions. Recommendations were for a watchful waiting approach to allow for granulation of the defect. The patient presented for follow-up approximately 2 years later, with his parents reporting concerns for persistence of the lesion. He was also having issues with food trapping in the area of the defect. He was found to have an approximately 1-cm anterior midline tongue indentation (Figure 1), and surgical excision was recommended. Following surgical excision, histopathologic examination of the excised tract demonstrated squamous and respiratory mucosa with regional striated muscle bundles, smooth muscle, adipose tissue, and minor salivary glands.

case_info.explanation: The foregut gives rise to the pharynx, lower respiratory tract, and upper gastrointestinal tract, including the esophagus, stomach, duodenum, and hepatobiliary system. Foregut duplication cysts, also known as enteric duplication cysts (EDCs), result from abnormal embryologic development (Figure 2). Their precise etiology is not well understood, and multiple theories have been proposed to explain their origin. To our knowledge, there is no single unifying explanation for the variety of EDCs that can occur throughout the body. The aberrant budding theory is commonly used to explain esophageal and bronchogenic cysts. According to this theory, outpouchings develop from the primitive gut tube and become isolated from the main tract. These outpouchings are lined with secretory epithelium, allowing fluid accumulation and cyst formation. Another proposed mechanism involves errors during the recanalization of the primitive gut tube. In this scenario, failure of recanalization results in the formation of isolated tubular structures that retain fluid and persist during development. The split notochord theory is the most widely accepted embryologic explanation for enteric cysts in general. It suggests that an abnormal connection forms between the notochord and the primitive gut tube that results in persistent adhesions and anomalous development. This theory is useful in explaining neurenteric cysts; however, it does not readily explain the presence of cysts within the oral cavity.1-3 EDCs, or enterocystomas, can theoretically occur anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract. Most frequently, they are found in the thorax or abdomen, particularly near the esophagus or small bowel.4In contrast, cysts of the head and neck region are exceedingly rare, accounting for fewer than 1% of all EDCs. Among these rare head and neck occurrences, the oral cavity is the most common location.4When in the oral cavity, they can also be known as lingual choristomas.5 Most cysts (approximately 80%) present before age 2 years. Prenatal ultrasonography may detect enteric duplications as early as 16 weeks of gestational age but is only possible in 20% to 30% of cases.2,5Postnatally, magnetic resonance imaging is the imaging modality of choice. It provides soft tissue contrast and can delineate the extent of the cyst, its relationship to adjacent structures, and the presence of any associated anomalies. However, EDCs cannot be reliably distinguished from dermoid cysts or other cystic lesions based on imaging alone. In one study that evaluated 6 pediatric patients with oral cavity EDCs, all were misdiagnosed before surgical excision.3,5 Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation. Classically, 3 criteria must be met: (1) the cyst must be surrounded by a smooth muscle layer; (2) it must be lined with gastrointestinal, gastric, or respiratory epithelium; and (3) it must be attached to a structure derived from the foregut.2Therefore, a diagnosis can only be made after surgical excision or biopsy, when tissue can be evaluated microscopically. Clinically, oral EDCs may be asymptomatic or may present with airway compromise, respiratory distress, or feeding difficulties, particularly in neonates and infants. In emergent situations, needle decompression can provide temporary relief, but complete surgical excision is the definitive treatment. Even when a cyst has ruptured, excision is still recommended. Retention of the cyst may result in progressive enlargement, mass effect, or recurrent infection. While cyst recurrence is rare, it is possible if the secretory epithelium is not completely removed.3 In summary, oral foregut duplication cysts are rare congenital anomalies that present diagnostic and management challenges. Awareness of their embryologic basis, clinical presentation, and imaging limitations is essential for prompt diagnosis and appropriate surgical treatment. Early recognition and excision lead to excellent outcomes and reduce the risk of complications or recurrence. The patient’s postoperative course was uncomplicated. At follow-up, he had resumed a regular diet and was no longer having issues with food trapping.

case_info.explanation: The foregut gives rise to the pharynx, lower respiratory tract, and upper gastrointestinal tract, including the esophagus, stomach, duodenum, and hepatobiliary system. Foregut duplication cysts, also known as enteric duplication cysts (EDCs), result from abnormal embryologic development (Figure 2). Their precise etiology is not well understood, and multiple theories have been proposed to explain their origin. To our knowledge, there is no single unifying explanation for the variety of EDCs that can occur throughout the body. The aberrant budding theory is commonly used to explain esophageal and bronchogenic cysts. According to this theory, outpouchings develop from the primitive gut tube and become isolated from the main tract. These outpouchings are lined with secretory epithelium, allowing fluid accumulation and cyst formation. Another proposed mechanism involves errors during the recanalization of the primitive gut tube. In this scenario, failure of recanalization results in the formation of isolated tubular structures that retain fluid and persist during development. The split notochord theory is the most widely accepted embryologic explanation for enteric cysts in general. It suggests that an abnormal connection forms between the notochord and the primitive gut tube that results in persistent adhesions and anomalous development. This theory is useful in explaining neurenteric cysts; however, it does not readily explain the presence of cysts within the oral cavity.1-3 EDCs, or enterocystomas, can theoretically occur anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract. Most frequently, they are found in the thorax or abdomen, particularly near the esophagus or small bowel.4In contrast, cysts of the head and neck region are exceedingly rare, accounting for fewer than 1% of all EDCs. Among these rare head and neck occurrences, the oral cavity is the most common location.4When in the oral cavity, they can also be known as lingual choristomas.5 Most cysts (approximately 80%) present before age 2 years. Prenatal ultrasonography may detect enteric duplications as early as 16 weeks of gestational age but is only possible in 20% to 30% of cases.2,5Postnatally, magnetic resonance imaging is the imaging modality of choice. It provides soft tissue contrast and can delineate the extent of the cyst, its relationship to adjacent structures, and the presence of any associated anomalies. However, EDCs cannot be reliably distinguished from dermoid cysts or other cystic lesions based on imaging alone. In one study that evaluated 6 pediatric patients with oral cavity EDCs, all were misdiagnosed before surgical excision.3,5 Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation. Classically, 3 criteria must be met: (1) the cyst must be surrounded by a smooth muscle layer; (2) it must be lined with gastrointestinal, gastric, or respiratory epithelium; and (3) it must be attached to a structure derived from the foregut.2Therefore, a diagnosis can only be made after surgical excision or biopsy, when tissue can be evaluated microscopically. Clinically, oral EDCs may be asymptomatic or may present with airway compromise, respiratory distress, or feeding difficulties, particularly in neonates and infants. In emergent situations, needle decompression can provide temporary relief, but complete surgical excision is the definitive treatment. Even when a cyst has ruptured, excision is still recommended. Retention of the cyst may result in progressive enlargement, mass effect, or recurrent infection. While cyst recurrence is rare, it is possible if the secretory epithelium is not completely removed.3 In summary, oral foregut duplication cysts are rare congenital anomalies that present diagnostic and management challenges. Awareness of their embryologic basis, clinical presentation, and imaging limitations is essential for prompt diagnosis and appropriate surgical treatment. Early recognition and excision lead to excellent outcomes and reduce the risk of complications or recurrence. The patient’s postoperative course was uncomplicated. At follow-up, he had resumed a regular diet and was no longer having issues with food trapping.

case_info.explanation: The foregut gives rise to the pharynx, lower respiratory tract, and upper gastrointestinal tract, including the esophagus, stomach, duodenum, and hepatobiliary system. Foregut duplication cysts, also known as enteric duplication cysts (EDCs), result from abnormal embryologic development (Figure 2). Their precise etiology is not well understood, and multiple theories have been proposed to explain their origin. To our knowledge, there is no single unifying explanation for the variety of EDCs that can occur throughout the body. The aberrant budding theory is commonly used to explain esophageal and bronchogenic cysts. According to this theory, outpouchings develop from the primitive gut tube and become isolated from the main tract. These outpouchings are lined with secretory epithelium, allowing fluid accumulation and cyst formation. Another proposed mechanism involves errors during the recanalization of the primitive gut tube. In this scenario, failure of recanalization results in the formation of isolated tubular structures that retain fluid and persist during development. The split notochord theory is the most widely accepted embryologic explanation for enteric cysts in general. It suggests that an abnormal connection forms between the notochord and the primitive gut tube that results in persistent adhesions and anomalous development. This theory is useful in explaining neurenteric cysts; however, it does not readily explain the presence of cysts within the oral cavity.1-3 EDCs, or enterocystomas, can theoretically occur anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract. Most frequently, they are found in the thorax or abdomen, particularly near the esophagus or small bowel.4In contrast, cysts of the head and neck region are exceedingly rare, accounting for fewer than 1% of all EDCs. Among these rare head and neck occurrences, the oral cavity is the most common location.4When in the oral cavity, they can also be known as lingual choristomas.5 Most cysts (approximately 80%) present before age 2 years. Prenatal ultrasonography may detect enteric duplications as early as 16 weeks of gestational age but is only possible in 20% to 30% of cases.2,5Postnatally, magnetic resonance imaging is the imaging modality of choice. It provides soft tissue contrast and can delineate the extent of the cyst, its relationship to adjacent structures, and the presence of any associated anomalies. However, EDCs cannot be reliably distinguished from dermoid cysts or other cystic lesions based on imaging alone. In one study that evaluated 6 pediatric patients with oral cavity EDCs, all were misdiagnosed before surgical excision.3,5 Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation. Classically, 3 criteria must be met: (1) the cyst must be surrounded by a smooth muscle layer; (2) it must be lined with gastrointestinal, gastric, or respiratory epithelium; and (3) it must be attached to a structure derived from the foregut.2Therefore, a diagnosis can only be made after surgical excision or biopsy, when tissue can be evaluated microscopically. Clinically, oral EDCs may be asymptomatic or may present with airway compromise, respiratory distress, or feeding difficulties, particularly in neonates and infants. In emergent situations, needle decompression can provide temporary relief, but complete surgical excision is the definitive treatment. Even when a cyst has ruptured, excision is still recommended. Retention of the cyst may result in progressive enlargement, mass effect, or recurrent infection. While cyst recurrence is rare, it is possible if the secretory epithelium is not completely removed.3 In summary, oral foregut duplication cysts are rare congenital anomalies that present diagnostic and management challenges. Awareness of their embryologic basis, clinical presentation, and imaging limitations is essential for prompt diagnosis and appropriate surgical treatment. Early recognition and excision lead to excellent outcomes and reduce the risk of complications or recurrence. The patient’s postoperative course was uncomplicated. At follow-up, he had resumed a regular diet and was no longer having issues with food trapping.

     after the AI's message.

   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

   Definition:

     message.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.

case_info.explanation: The foregut gives rise to the pharynx, lower respiratory tract, and upper gastrointestinal tract, including the esophagus, stomach, duodenum, and hepatobiliary system. Foregut duplication cysts, also known as enteric duplication cysts (EDCs), result from abnormal embryologic development (Figure 2). Their precise etiology is not well understood, and multiple theories have been proposed to explain their origin. To our knowledge, there is no single unifying explanation for the variety of EDCs that can occur throughout the body. The aberrant budding theory is commonly used to explain esophageal and bronchogenic cysts. According to this theory, outpouchings develop from the primitive gut tube and become isolated from the main tract. These outpouchings are lined with secretory epithelium, allowing fluid accumulation and cyst formation. Another proposed mechanism involves errors during the recanalization of the primitive gut tube. In this scenario, failure of recanalization results in the formation of isolated tubular structures that retain fluid and persist during development. The split notochord theory is the most widely accepted embryologic explanation for enteric cysts in general. It suggests that an abnormal connection forms between the notochord and the primitive gut tube that results in persistent adhesions and anomalous development. This theory is useful in explaining neurenteric cysts; however, it does not readily explain the presence of cysts within the oral cavity.1-3 EDCs, or enterocystomas, can theoretically occur anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract. Most frequently, they are found in the thorax or abdomen, particularly near the esophagus or small bowel.4In contrast, cysts of the head and neck region are exceedingly rare, accounting for fewer than 1% of all EDCs. Among these rare head and neck occurrences, the oral cavity is the most common location.4When in the oral cavity, they can also be known as lingual choristomas.5 Most cysts (approximately 80%) present before age 2 years. Prenatal ultrasonography may detect enteric duplications as early as 16 weeks of gestational age but is only possible in 20% to 30% of cases.2,5Postnatally, magnetic resonance imaging is the imaging modality of choice. However, EDCs cannot be reliably distinguished from dermoid cysts or other cystic lesions based on imaging alone. In one study that evaluated 6 pediatric patients with oral cavity EDCs, all were misdiagnosed before surgical excision.3,5 Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation. Classically, 3 criteria must be met: (1) the cyst must be surrounded by a smooth muscle layer; (2) it must be lined with gastrointestinal, gastric, or respiratory epithelium; and (3) it must be attached to a structure derived from the foregut.2Therefore, a diagnosis can only be made after surgical excision or biopsy, when tissue can be evaluated microscopically. Clinically, oral EDCs may be asymptomatic or may present with airway compromise, respiratory distress, or feeding difficulties, particularly in neonates and infants. In emergent situations, needle decompression can provide temporary relief, but complete surgical excision is the definitive treatment. Even when a cyst has ruptured, excision is still recommended. Retention of the cyst may result in progressive enlargement, mass effect, or recurrent infection. While cyst recurrence is rare, it is possible if the secretory epithelium is not completely removed.3 In summary, oral foregut duplication cysts are rare congenital anomalies that present diagnostic and management challenges. Awareness of their embryologic basis, clinical presentation, and imaging limitations is essential for prompt diagnosis and appropriate surgical treatment. case_info.explanation: The foregut gives rise to the pharynx, lower respiratory tract, and upper gastrointestinal tract, including the esophagus, stomach, duodenum, and hepatobiliary system. Foregut duplication cysts, also known as enteric duplication cysts (EDCs), result from abnormal embryologic development (Figure 2). Their precise etiology is not well understood, and multiple theories have been proposed to explain their origin. To our knowledge, there is no single unifying explanation for the variety of EDCs that can occur throughout the body. The aberrant budding theory is commonly used to explain esophageal and bronchogenic cysts. According to this theory, outpouchings develop from the primitive gut tube and become isolated from the main tract. These outpouchings are lined with secretory epithelium, allowing fluid accumulation and cyst formation. Another proposed mechanism involves errors during the recanalization of the primitive gut tube. In this scenario, failure of recanalization results in the formation of isolated tubular structures that retain fluid and persist during development. The split notochord theory is the most widely accepted embryologic explanation for enteric cysts in general. It suggests that an abnormal connection forms between the notochord and the primitive gut tube that results in persistent adhesions and anomalous development. This theory is useful in explaining neurenteric cysts; however, it does not readily explain the presence of cysts within the oral cavity.1-3 EDCs, or enterocystomas, can theoretically occur anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract. Most frequently, they are found in the thorax or abdomen, particularly near the esophagus or small bowel.4In contrast, cysts of the head and neck region are exceedingly rare, accounting for fewer than 1% of all EDCs. Among these rare head and neck occurrences, the oral cavity is the most common location.4When in the oral cavity, they can also be known as lingual choristomas.5 Most cysts (approximately 80%) present before age 2 years. Prenatal ultrasonography may detect enteric duplications as early as 16 weeks of gestational age but is only possible in 20% to 30% of cases.2,5Postnatally, magnetic resonance imaging is the imaging modality of choice. It provides soft tissue contrast and can delineate the extent of the cyst, its relationship to adjacent structures, and the presence of any associated anomalies. However, EDCs cannot be reliably distinguished from dermoid cysts or other cystic lesions based on imaging alone. In one study that evaluated 6 pediatric patients with oral cavity EDCs, all were misdiagnosed before surgical excision.3,5 Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation. Classically, 3 criteria must be met: (1) the cyst must be surrounded by a smooth muscle layer; (2) it must be lined with gastrointestinal, gastric, or respiratory epithelium; and (3) it must be attached to a structure derived from the foregut.2Therefore, a diagnosis can only be made after surgical excision or biopsy, when tissue can be evaluated microscopically. Clinically, oral EDCs may be asymptomatic or may present with airway compromise, respiratory distress, or feeding difficulties, particularly in neonates and infants. In emergent situations, needle decompression can provide temporary relief, but complete surgical excision is the definitive treatment. Even when a cyst has ruptured, excision is still recommended. Retention of the cyst may result in progressive enlargement, mass effect, or recurrent infection. While cyst recurrence is rare, it is possible if the secretory epithelium is not completely removed.3 In summary, oral foregut duplication cysts are rare congenital anomalies that present diagnostic and management challenges. Awareness of their embryologic basis, clinical presentation, and imaging limitations is essential for prompt diagnosis and appropriate surgical treatment. Early recognition and excision lead to excellent outcomes and reduce the risk of complications or recurrence. The patient’s postoperative course was uncomplicated. At follow-up, he had resumed a regular diet and was no longer having issues with food trapping.

He was also having issues with food trapping in the area of the defect. He was found to have an approximately 1-cm anterior midline tongue indentation (Figure 1), and surgical excision was recommended. case_info.scenario: A male infant aged 2 weeks presented to an otolaryngology clinic for evaluation of a tongue lesion. The patient was born at 39 weeks of gestation via caesarean delivery that was complicated by preeclampsia. Prenatal ultrasonography and subsequent magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated concern for a tongue cyst. At birth, a small midline tongue defect was noted, for which the patient was referred to an ear, nose, and throat clinic. At the time of the initial evaluation, he was feeding well and gaining weight appropriately. He was found to have a shallow, midline tongue depression with no discrete masses or lesions. Recommendations were for a watchful waiting approach to allow for granulation of the defect. The patient presented for follow-up approximately 2 years later, with his parents reporting concerns for persistence of the lesion. He was also having issues with food trapping in the area of the defect. He was found to have an approximately 1-cm anterior midline tongue indentation (Figure 1), and surgical excision was recommended. Following surgical excision, histopathologic examination of the excised tract demonstrated squamous and respiratory mucosa with regional striated muscle bundles, smooth muscle, adipose tissue, and minor salivary glands.
case_info.caption: Preoperative photograph of midline tongue defect.
case_info.explanation: The foregut gives rise to the pharynx, lower respiratory tract, and upper gastrointestinal tract, including the esophagus, stomach, duodenum, and hepatobiliary system. Foregut duplication cysts, also known as enteric duplication cysts (EDCs), result from abnormal embryologic development (Figure 2). Their precise etiology is not well understood, and multiple theories have been proposed to explain their origin. To our knowledge, there is no single unifying explanation for the variety of EDCs that can occur throughout the body. The aberrant budding theory is commonly used to explain esophageal and bronchogenic cysts. According to this theory, outpouchings develop from the primitive gut tube and become isolated from the main tract. These outpouchings are lined with secretory epithelium, allowing fluid accumulation and cyst formation. Another proposed mechanism involves errors during the recanalization of the primitive gut tube. In this scenario, failure of recanalization results in the formation of isolated tubular structures that retain fluid and persist during development. The split notochord theory is the most widely accepted embryologic explanation for enteric cysts in general. It suggests that an abnormal connection forms between the notochord and the primitive gut tube that results in persistent adhesions and anomalous development. This theory is useful in explaining neurenteric cysts; however, it does not readily explain the presence of cysts within the oral cavity.1-3 EDCs, or enterocystomas, can theoretically occur anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract. Most frequently, they are found in the thorax or abdomen, particularly near the esophagus or small bowel.4In contrast, cysts of the head and neck region are exceedingly rare, accounting for fewer than 1% of all EDCs. Among these rare head and neck occurrences, the oral cavity is the most common location.4When in the oral cavity, they can also be known as lingual choristomas.5 Most cysts (approximately 80%) present before age 2 years. Prenatal ultrasonography may detect enteric duplications as early as 16 weeks of gestational age but is only possible in 20% to 30% of cases.2,5Postnatally, magnetic resonance imaging is the imaging modality of choice. It provides soft tissue contrast and can delineate the extent of the cyst, its relationship to adjacent structures, and the presence of any associated anomalies. However, EDCs cannot be reliably distinguished from dermoid cysts or other cystic lesions based on imaging alone. In one study that evaluated 6 pediatric patients with oral cavity EDCs, all were misdiagnosed before surgical excision.3,5 Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation. Classically, 3 criteria must be met: (1) the cyst must be surrounded by a smooth muscle layer; (2) it must be lined with gastrointestinal, gastric, or respiratory epithelium; and (3) it must be attached to a structure derived from the foregut.2Therefore, a diagnosis can only be made after surgical excision or biopsy, when tissue can be evaluated microscopically. Clinically, oral EDCs may be asymptomatic or may present with airway compromise, respiratory distress, or feeding difficulties, particularly in neonates and infants. In emergent situations, needle decompression can provide temporary relief, but complete surgical excision is the definitive treatment. Even when a cyst has ruptured, excision is still recommended. Retention of the cyst may result in progressive enlargement, mass effect, or recurrent infection. While cyst recurrence is rare, it is possible if the secretory epithelium is not completely removed.3 In summary, oral foregut duplication cysts are rare congenital anomalies that present diagnostic and management challenges. Awareness of their embryologic basis, clinical presentation, and imaging limitations is essential for prompt diagnosis and appropriate surgical treatment. Early recognition and excision lead to excellent outcomes and reduce the risk of complications or recurrence. The patient’s postoperative course was uncomplicated. At follow-up, he had resumed a regular diet and was no longer having issues with food trapping.

case_info.explanation: The foregut gives rise to the pharynx, lower respiratory tract, and upper gastrointestinal tract, including the esophagus, stomach, duodenum, and hepatobiliary system. Foregut duplication cysts, also known as enteric duplication cysts (EDCs), result from abnormal embryologic development (Figure 2). Their precise etiology is not well understood, and multiple theories have been proposed to explain their origin. To our knowledge, there is no single unifying explanation for the variety of EDCs that can occur throughout the body. The aberrant budding theory is commonly used to explain esophageal and bronchogenic cysts. According to this theory, outpouchings develop from the primitive gut tube and become isolated from the main tract. These outpouchings are lined with secretory epithelium, allowing fluid accumulation and cyst formation. Another proposed mechanism involves errors during the recanalization of the primitive gut tube. In this scenario, failure of recanalization results in the formation of isolated tubular structures that retain fluid and persist during development. The split notochord theory is the most widely accepted embryologic explanation for enteric cysts in general. It suggests that an abnormal connection forms between the notochord and the primitive gut tube that results in persistent adhesions and anomalous development. This theory is useful in explaining neurenteric cysts; however, it does not readily explain the presence of cysts within the oral cavity.1-3 EDCs, or enterocystomas, can theoretically occur anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract. Most frequently, they are found in the thorax or abdomen, particularly near the esophagus or small bowel.4In contrast, cysts of the head and neck region are exceedingly rare, accounting for fewer than 1% of all EDCs. Among these rare head and neck occurrences, the oral cavity is the most common location.4When in the oral cavity, they can also be known as lingual choristomas.5 Most cysts (approximately 80%) present before age 2 years. Prenatal ultrasonography may detect enteric duplications as early as 16 weeks of gestational age but is only possible in 20% to 30% of cases.2,5Postnatally, magnetic resonance imaging is the imaging modality of choice. It provides soft tissue contrast and can delineate the extent of the cyst, its relationship to adjacent structures, and the presence of any associated anomalies. However, EDCs cannot be reliably distinguished from dermoid cysts or other cystic lesions based on imaging alone. In one study that evaluated 6 pediatric patients with oral cavity EDCs, all were misdiagnosed before surgical excision.3,5 Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation. Classically, 3 criteria must be met: (1) the cyst must be surrounded by a smooth muscle layer; (2) it must be lined with gastrointestinal, gastric, or respiratory epithelium; and (3) it must be attached to a structure derived from the foregut.2Therefore, a diagnosis can only be made after surgical excision or biopsy, when tissue can be evaluated microscopically. Clinically, oral EDCs may be asymptomatic or may present with airway compromise, respiratory distress, or feeding difficulties, particularly in neonates and infants. In emergent situations, needle decompression can provide temporary relief, but complete surgical excision is the definitive treatment. Even when a cyst has ruptured, excision is still recommended. Retention of the cyst may result in progressive enlargement, mass effect, or recurrent infection. While cyst recurrence is rare, it is possible if the secretory epithelium is not completely removed.3 In summary, oral foregut duplication cysts are rare congenital anomalies that present diagnostic and management challenges. Awareness of their embryologic basis, clinical presentation, and imaging limitations is essential for prompt diagnosis and appropriate surgical treatment. Early recognition and excision lead to excellent outcomes and reduce the risk of complications or recurrence. The patient’s postoperative course was uncomplicated. At follow-up, he had resumed a regular diet and was no longer having issues with food trapping.

case_info.explanation: The foregut gives rise to the pharynx, lower respiratory tract, and upper gastrointestinal tract, including the esophagus, stomach, duodenum, and hepatobiliary system. Foregut duplication cysts, also known as enteric duplication cysts (EDCs), result from abnormal embryologic development (Figure 2). Their precise etiology is not well understood, and multiple theories have been proposed to explain their origin. To our knowledge, there is no single unifying explanation for the variety of EDCs that can occur throughout the body. The aberrant budding theory is commonly used to explain esophageal and bronchogenic cysts. According to this theory, outpouchings develop from the primitive gut tube and become isolated from the main tract. These outpouchings are lined with secretory epithelium, allowing fluid accumulation and cyst formation. Another proposed mechanism involves errors during the recanalization of the primitive gut tube. In this scenario, failure of recanalization results in the formation of isolated tubular structures that retain fluid and persist during development. The split notochord theory is the most widely accepted embryologic explanation for enteric cysts in general. It suggests that an abnormal connection forms between the notochord and the primitive gut tube that results in persistent adhesions and anomalous development. This theory is useful in explaining neurenteric cysts; however, it does not readily explain the presence of cysts within the oral cavity.1-3 EDCs, or enterocystomas, can theoretically occur anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract. Most frequently, they are found in the thorax or abdomen, particularly near the esophagus or small bowel.4In contrast, cysts of the head and neck region are exceedingly rare, accounting for fewer than 1% of all EDCs. Among these rare head and neck occurrences, the oral cavity is the most common location.4When in the oral cavity, they can also be known as lingual choristomas.5 Most cysts (approximately 80%) present before age 2 years. Prenatal ultrasonography may detect enteric duplications as early as 16 weeks of gestational age but is only possible in 20% to 30% of cases.2,5Postnatally, magnetic resonance imaging is the imaging modality of choice. It provides soft tissue contrast and can delineate the extent of the cyst, its relationship to adjacent structures, and the presence of any associated anomalies. However, EDCs cannot be reliably distinguished from dermoid cysts or other cystic lesions based on imaging alone. In one study that evaluated 6 pediatric patients with oral cavity EDCs, all were misdiagnosed before surgical excision.3,5 Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation. Classically, 3 criteria must be met: (1) the cyst must be surrounded by a smooth muscle layer; (2) it must be lined with gastrointestinal, gastric, or respiratory epithelium; and (3) it must be attached to a structure derived from the foregut.2Therefore, a diagnosis can only be made after surgical excision or biopsy, when tissue can be evaluated microscopically. Clinically, oral EDCs may be asymptomatic or may present with airway compromise, respiratory distress, or feeding difficulties, particularly in neonates and infants. In emergent situations, needle decompression can provide temporary relief, but complete surgical excision is the definitive treatment. Even when a cyst has ruptured, excision is still recommended. Retention of the cyst may result in progressive enlargement, mass effect, or recurrent infection. While cyst recurrence is rare, it is possible if the secretory epithelium is not completely removed.3 In summary, oral foregut duplication cysts are rare congenital anomalies that present diagnostic and management challenges. Awareness of their embryologic basis, clinical presentation, and imaging limitations is essential for prompt diagnosis and appropriate surgical treatment. Early recognition and excision lead to excellent outcomes and reduce the risk of complications or recurrence. The patient’s postoperative course was uncomplicated. At follow-up, he had resumed a regular diet and was no longer having issues with food trapping.
